pages.x: In the cool, fertile highlands of central Kenya, British settlers had taken the best farmland, and Kikuyu families were squeezed onto crowded reserves, or worked as squatters on white farms. Africans had almost no say in how the colony was run. In the late 1940s a secret movement began binding its members by oath to fight for land and freedom.

After a wave of killings, among them a senior chief loyal to the British, the governor, Sir Evelyn Baring, declared a state of emergency on 20 October 1952. That night police arrested Jomo Kenyatta and other African leaders, and thousands of young Kikuyu fled to the forests of the Aberdares and Mount Kenya to fight.

Kenyatta, the best-known African leader in Kenya, had studied in London and written a book about his people. The British tried him at a remote town, Kapenguria, as the head of Mau Mau, and in 1953 sentenced him to seven years of hard labour. He always denied leading it, and a key witness later admitted he had been paid to lie.

The war was also a civil war among the Kikuyu. On the night of 26 March 1953 Mau Mau fighters attacked Lari, a settlement of families loyal to the government, and killed over 70 people, many of them women and children. In revenge, the security forces and the loyalist Home Guard killed many suspects. Both sides used terror.
pages.of: killed in one night at Lari

pages.x: To cut the fighters off from their people, the British moved over a million Kikuyu into fenced and guarded villages, and held tens of thousands in detention camps without trial, where many were beaten and tortured to make them give up the oath. More than a thousand Kenyans were hanged.
pages.of: Kenyans hanged by the colonial courts

pages.x: The most famous forest leader was Dedan Kimathi, who called himself a field marshal and wrote letters to the newspapers from the Aberdares. After years on the run he was wounded and captured near Nyeri in October 1956, and hanged in Nairobi in 1957. By then the revolt was broken.

On 3 March 1959, at Hola camp, guards beat eleven detainees to death for refusing to work. The officials first said they had died from drinking bad water. When the truth came out it caused an uproar in Britain's parliament, and helped convince the government that it had to give up Kenya.
pages.of: detainees beaten to death at Hola

pages.x: The emergency ended in January 1960, and that same month talks in London opened the way to African majority rule. Kenyatta was freed in 1961, and on 12 December 1963 Kenya became independent, with the man the British had jailed as the leader of Mau Mau as its first prime minister.

More than 11,000 rebels were killed, against about 200 soldiers and police, and some 1,800 African civilians killed by the rebels. Mau Mau stayed banned in Kenya until 2003. In 2013 Britain, sued by elderly survivors of the camps, expressed regret for their torture and paid them compensation.
pts: A revolt over land and freedom
Over a million Kikuyu moved behind wire
